content:
There's an old saying in the photography world: the best camera is the one you have with you. The iPhone is certainly the camera most of us carry in our pockets most of the time, which is clearly a huge advantage for things like shooting kids and social events. But a recent video project has highlighted another benefit.

I really enjoy taking an evening walk through London, and I often use my iPhone to take photos and shoot video. At first I was doing it purely for my own enjoyment, but then I realised these clips could serve as B-roll footage for a video project...

My current project is experimental in nature — it's testing the practicality of 'Cinematic mode', and I've lamented previously that Apple seems to have stopped development on it. Once I finish next week, I'll share the results with everyone.

I wanted to follow a fairly specific format, where the interview segments needed to be cut together with very short landscape B-roll. In principle, these cutaways could be filmed anywhere in London, but since the main shoot was taking place by the river, I really wanted all the B-roll to be of the Thames. I needed four clips, and after a bit of searching through my iPhone videos I found suitable material.

The clip above also highlights another appealing aspect. If the footage happens to include passers-by who can be identified, I'll go over afterwards and show them the clip, asking if it's okay to use it. (This isn't a legal requirement in the UK, but I feel it's a matter of courtesy.) On many occasions they'll proactively ask for a copy. If they're using an iPhone, I'll share it with them instantly via AirDrop — quick and easy; for Android users, WhatsApp serves as a backup.

The iPhone's stabilisation has really been a huge help. Sometimes I'm not planning to film anything, but I spot a lovely scene during a walk and grab a handheld shot on the spur of the moment. Although I'll try to steady the camera by leaning against a wall, railing or lamppost, generally speaking the footage comes out looking as stable as if it had been shot on a tripod. (If I'm planning to take some video opportunistically during a walk, I'll also bring a small GorillaPod tripod along.)

Another major advantage of the iPhone is its foolproof operation. If I had to manually set exposure, white balance, ND filters and so on, I'd probably not bother — especially when walking with other people, as the time spent fiddling with settings would disrupt the outing. But asking someone to wait roughly 20 seconds doesn't feel like much of a drag.

If I want to stay in one spot for an extended period, shooting time-lapse video with the iPhone is also very straightforward. Once you've started recording you can stop at any time, and the iPhone adjusts automatically to give you a clip of a suitable length. In my old flat, I used to regularly leave the iPhone by the window, start a time-lapse at sunset, then get on with my own thing. Several of those clips became excellent B-roll for the video project.

Of course, if you zoom in pixel by pixel, the limitations of the iPhone's small sensor start to show — particularly in low-light conditions. But most YouTube viewers today watch on a phone or laptop, so for the most part the image quality is already more than adequate.

Whether 'Cinematic mode' footage holds up just as well remains to be seen, and I'll be relying on everyone to give me their feedback next week. But overall, being able to slip such a powerful camera into a pocket and pull it out whenever, wherever, has been a genuinely delightful surprise.
